problems: The three Gregory lines are anger, war and hell. The reveal paints a warm woman who laughs loudly and sobbed at her mother's funeral as a hard-liner. Gregory also disagrees with her on laughter, which is not shown.

Gregory's war line is not about a just war. It praises wars fought 'for the sake of extending the republic in which we see that God is worshipped', which is more than she holds (her husband preaches religious liberty). It is also cut off mid-sentence: 'the name of Christ may be …'.
Gregory's anger line is archaic and needs Phinehas and Eli explained: 'quickened against himself the stirrings of the vengeance of the Most High to an implacable force' will lose most readers.
Origen's war line opens 'And none fight better for the king than we do', which reads at first as agreement. The disagreement only comes in the second sentence.

Origen's 'deeper' line ('the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally') is unfair out of context. In the same part of On First Principles he says the historically true passages far outnumber the purely spiritual ones.
War and hell appear in both her kindred and her sparring lists. Shown once as a face-off (Gregory said this, Origen said that) it would be the best moment of the reveal. Shown twice it just repeats.
Her 'nature' answer came from reading 'books' as the Bible. Draft 2's 'as from any book' makes that reading more likely, not less.

Antony's laugh line never mentions laughing. It is cropped from the story of the hunter who saw Antony relaxing with the brothers. 'So it is also in the work of God' refers to a bow the reader has not been told about.

Antony's calm line is Athanasius describing Antony's face, not Antony's own words. It also says he was not 'possessed by laughter', which contradicts the laugh line shown just above it in the same reveal.
Antony's dreams line is about telling holy visions from demonic ones. It does not show that God speaks through dreams.
Her 'calm' agree was a misreading (staying calm on shift), and the Antony match partly rests on it.

Because none of the three lines clearly shows agreement, she cannot see why Antony is her match. Antony leaving family and land may also sting someone who gave up the convent for her family. That could be moving, but only if the reveal earns it.

Jerome's tears line is a fairness risk. In the same letter to Paula he weeps himself and says he asks only for moderation in grief. His target is grief 'without limits'. Putting him at the far pole on weeping for the dead overstates him.
Jerome's calm line starts mid-sentence ('a state in which the mind ceases to be agitated…'). Without context the reader cannot tell he is mocking the ideal.
The dates for Jerome and Antony are too scholarly for this page (birthplace on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia; 'the Life says he died about 105 years old').
Isaac's calling line is unreadable. It has a stray ',If', starts mid-story, is cut off at 'should I …', and never says who is begging whom.
Isaac's solitude line is stiff: 'Compare not all powers and signs … with a man's consciously sitting in solitude'.

Basil's mystery line ('to investigate syllables is not to shoot wide of the mark') is about the wording of a doxology. It does not show Basil wanting every question about God pursued, and it misrepresents him. Against Eunomius and in Letter 234 he insisted that God's essence is beyond our knowing, so the far-pole coding on this statement is probably wrong.
Basil's laugh line is cut mid-sentence ('for …').
Basil against Isaac on solitude is the real clash, and it is a fun one ('Whose feet then wilt thou wash?'). That line should lead, and the mystery line should go.
Isaac's hope for all, which is what this person privately holds, appears only in the hook. That is fine, since he answered Not sure.

None of the three Augustine lines touch what she said felt most like her: dreams, tears and the body. Augustine weeping for his mother in Confessions 9 would land far harder than the line about Platonists.
Augustine's learning line is cut mid-phrase ('from those who have unlawful …') and leans on the 'spoiling the Egyptians' image without its setup.
Cassian's learning line is a personal lament that his memory is full of the poems he read as a boy. It does not say that wisdom from outsiders is worthless, so the clash is not shown.
Cassian's quiet line is long and cut off ('endeavour rather to perform than to …').
Cassian is unknown to her. The hook (losing his temper at his pen, knife and flint) carries it well.
Basil disagrees with him on five of the thirteen statements they share: laughter (he laughs easily), wealth, surplus, mystery and nature. That is a lot for a kindred spirit.
Basil's church-discipline line is long, cut off ('involves the …') and depends on 1 Corinthians 5. He would follow it, but most players would not.
Origen's dreams line is cut off just before the word 'dream' ('either in a waking vision or …'), so it does not show dreams at all.
Origen's 'deeper' line has the same fairness problem noted for P1.
Among equal-weight clashes the lines are picked in play order, so universalism, his strongest theological clash with Origen, is skipped in favour of dreams.
people.better: Augustine of Hippo. His profile matches Augustine's own: a confessional Reformed student who strongly rejects 'becoming good is up to you' and universal salvation, strongly backs just war and righteous anger, and rejects the ideal of feeling nothing. Calvin quotes Augustine more than any other Father. The data ranks Augustine fifth mainly because it puts him at the far pole on church discipline (from his fight with the Donatists), which is questionable: Augustine excommunicated people and wrote on correction.

problems: Nyssa's body line from On Virginity is archaic and hard to follow: 'The inefficiency of the body from either cause will be that which it guards against'.

Nyssa's hope that all will be restored is the most moving match for her (she agreed, as hope), and his hook points straight at it, but it is not shown. Lines are chosen by answer strength, and her 'all' was only Agree.
Tertullian's tears line ('why should you grieve…') may sting a widow of three years. It is fair and it is his real view, which is what a sparring partner is for.
Origen's 'deeper' line has the fairness problem noted for P1: out of context it makes him deny the history in general.
Origen's lying line is cut off at 'Judith …', and its source label is cluttered: 'Stromateis , book 6 , quoted by Jerome in Apology against Rufinus'.

Gregory's learning line (Christ and Jupiter in one mouth) does not answer the statement without context. It rebukes a bishop for teaching pagan poetry. The source label is only '(Letters)': name the recipient.

Gregory's rulers line is a fairness risk. A few weeks later, in his letter to Mellitus, Gregory told the mission not to destroy the temples but to turn them into churches. Keep 'Make haste to extend the Christian faith among the peoples under your sway' and drop 'overturn the edifices of their temples'.
She noted that five statements assume God exists. The reveal still works well for her.

Tertullian on dreams ('almost the greater part of mankind get their knowledge of God from dreams') is a gift for her. His later embrace of the New Prophecy, and his being an African Christian, would delight her more, but the reveal says neither.
The second sentence of Tertullian's calling line (about quitting arts and trades) is confusing without the context of On Idolatry.
Nyssa's effort line ('the Divine good … is within each of us') does not show that becoming good is mostly up to you, so the clash is not visible.
Nyssa's 'all' line is cut off just before its key words ('to their primal …') and capitalises 'Sin' oddly.
Nyssa is unknown to her. The hook ('hoped even the devil would be healed') is what makes this pairing fun.
Origen's war line opens 'And none fight better for the king than we do', which a skimming reader takes as the opposite of his view.
Origen's 'deeper' line has the fairness problem noted for P1.
Gregory's learning line (Jupiter) needs context, as noted for P7.
Gregory's war line is cut off mid-sentence ('may be …') and argues for wars that spread Christian rule, not just war. As a sparring line for a pacifist it works, but end it on a full stop.
Gregory's rulers line has the Mellitus problem noted for P7.
Gregory shows P7 and P9 the same three lines, and Origen shows P1, P5 and P10 nearly the same three. Friends who compare results will notice.

His kindred spirit is at the opposite pole on the two statements that matter most to him. On war, Tertullian wrote in On Idolatry that the Lord, in disarming Peter, unbelted every soldier. On weeping for the dead, Tertullian argues against grieving, and this man lost a squadmate. The reveal hides both, and if he reads more about Tertullian the match will feel like a betrayal.

Tertullian's laugh line is about mocking heretics ('the truth may indulge in ridicule … it may play with its enemies'), not about a hearty laugh. It misreads both him and the statement, and the pro-laughter coding that rests on it is doubtful (On the Shows points the other way).
Tertullian's calm line is archaic ('the irascible and the concupiscible elements of our soul') and will not reach him. That is a pity, because the statement 'hit close' for him.
Origen's mystery line is an unreadable fragment. It starts mid-sentence and is cut off ('a subject of …').
people.better: Augustine of Hippo. In Letter 189 he tells Boniface, a serving general: 'Do not think that it is impossible for any one to please God while engaged in active military service.' In the Confessions he weeps openly for his friend and for his mother. In City of God 14.9 he calls a mind that feels nothing worse than all vices, which speaks straight to his note that feeling nothing was the worst part of coming home. He is also firm on hell and on grace. The centring shrinks exactly the shared answers (tears, laughter, emotion, the body) that make Augustine his match.

works: The hooks are the best thing on the page: specific, human and often funny (Origen's mother hiding his clothes, Augustine's pears, Cassian cursing his blunt knife and dull flint, Nyssa forging letters, Tertullian impatient in a book on patience). They make unfamiliar names vivid in one sentence.

When a match is right it is very right: Isaac the Syrian for the Orthodox convert, Gregory of Nyssa for the hopeful Methodist widow, Origen for the agnostic philosopher and the Quaker pacifist, and Tertullian on dreams for the Pentecostal shopkeeper. Each would give a real 'that's me'.

The sparring partner is nearly always the obvious opponent, and it is fun: Origen for conservative evangelicals (allegory, war, hell), Tertullian's 'What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' for the progressive, Jerome's 'detestable tears' and 'leave to worldlings the privileges of laughing' for the laughing, grieving nurse, and Gregory on war and state religion for the pacifist.
Showing the statement, the player's own answer and the Father's real words makes each claim checkable and ties the result to what the player said. That is the right shape.
The everyday statements work. People answered most of them in a second, and tears, dreams, laughter, war and government produced the strongest and clearest reactions.

Short, whole, vivid lines land hardest: 'Whose feet then wilt thou wash?', 'Love silence above all things', 'it is covetousness that is condemned, not gold', Tertullian on dreams, Jerome on tears. Every line should meet that bar.
Where one statement appears in both lists (P1: war and hell), the reveal turns into a natural face-off between two Fathers. That is the most shareable moment the format has.
change: Hand-pick each line: one whole sentence, 25 words at most, ending on a full stop, never cut off with '…'. The automatic 45-word cut in model.mjs cuts off the key word in at least five of these ten reveals (Origen 'waking vision or …', Nyssa 'primal …', Gregory 'may be …', Augustine 'unlawful …', Isaac 'should I …'). Where the Victorian translation is opaque (Gregory on Phinehas, Nyssa's On Virginity, Tertullian's 'irascible and concupiscible', Isaac's 'Compare not …'), use a plain modern rendering of the same sentence and mark it with the own-rendering flag the data already has.

Run a blind test on every cell: shown only the statement and the line, can a reader tell whether this person agrees or disagrees? These fail it: Antony on laughter (the bow story), Antony on dreams (holy visions against demons), Basil on mystery (syllables), Cassian on learning (his own cluttered memory), Gregory on learning (Jupiter), Nyssa on effort, Origen on mystery, Tertullian on laughter (mocking heretics), Isaac on calling. Replace the line or drop the cell.

Put a plain verdict in front of each quote, such as 'Gregory agrees:' or 'Origen disagrees:'. It is only the cell's sign, so nothing is invented, and it tells the reader how to read an old sentence before they start it.

Use only a person's own words. Antony's lines come from Athanasius's Life, and the calm line is Athanasius describing his face. Use sayings where Antony himself speaks, or label the line 'as Athanasius tells it'.

Choose lines by how telling they are, not by play order among ties. Use the centred weight the scorer already computes, and prefer statements the player answered Strongly and far from the usual answer. Today 'learning', 'deeper' and 'war' repeat across almost every reveal and push out the telling ones: Augustine's tears for P4, Nyssa's hope for all for P6, Origen's universalism for P5.

Guard the kindred spirit. Rule out anyone at the opposite extreme on two or more statements the player answered Strongly, and always show one honest 'where he would push back' line under the kindred. P10, a combat veteran matched with the Father who said Christ unbelted every soldier, is the failure this prevents. The push-back line also makes the match feel truer, not weaker.

Retest the centring. SHRINK 0.75 removes so much of the shared ground on popular statements (tears, laughter, emotion, the body) that a Father who shares a person's heart there loses to one who shares only the edgy positions (Augustine for P10 and P5). Try about 0.5, or centre only the Fathers' side, and rerun this test before the owner sees it.

Check these codings before the next test. Basil on mystery: Letter 234 and Against Eunomius say God's essence is beyond us, so he leans agree, not -2. Tertullian on laughter: the +1 rests on mocking heretics, and On the Shows points the other way. Jerome on tears: -2 is too strong, since he weeps in the very letter and asks only for moderation. Origen on the deeper meaning: use a line saying every passage has a spiritual sense, since On First Principles 4.3.4 says the historical passages far outnumber the others. Gregory on rulers: drop the temple clause he reversed in his letter to Mellitus. Augustine on church discipline: -2 from the Donatist fight may be too strong, since he excommunicated people and wrote on correction.

Fix these statements. 'nature': draft 2's 'as from any book' still includes the Bible, and 2 of 10 read it that way. Try 'You can learn as much about God outdoors as from reading and study.' 'surplus': it still reads as a political slogan to 4 of 10 conservatives. Try the Fathers' own framing: 'Giving to the poor is paying back what's theirs, not doing them a favour.' 'effort': 'mostly up to you' pushed every synergy-minded person (Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist, Quaker) to disagree, so it cannot separate Cassian from Augustine. Try 'The first step toward God has to come from you.' 'tell': 'your job' read as policing to 4 of 10. Try 'If a friend is doing something seriously wrong, you should say so.'
When a statement appears in both the kindred and the sparring lists, show it once as a face-off: 'On war: Gregory said …, Origen said …'. Make that block the share card.

Keep two or three verified lines per cell and rotate them. Origen shows P1, P5 and P10 almost the same three lines, and Gregory shows P7 and P9 the same three, so friends comparing results will see identical cards.

Trim the clutter. Dates like 'c. 330–379', with no 'traditional reckoning; some scholars prefer' and no birthplace. Hooks of 35 words at most (Gregory the Great's and Jerome's run past 60). Clean source labels: no ' , ' spacing, and name the recipient of every letter. Fix the stray ',If', the '--' and the capital in 'Sin'.
Give each 'also close' name a few words saying why (for example 'also close: John Cassian, on silence'). A bare name is a dead end, and a reason is a reason to click.
